introduction: These readings say that education brings out what is hidden in a human being as a jeweller brings a gem from the mine: character first, then knowledge; body, mind and spirit together; early, because habits harden; and by the learner's own effort, since capacity is given but not realized without it. They compare the teacher to a gardener and the heart to soil. Beside them stand Plato, Aristotle, Confucius and Mencius on nature and practice, the proverbs on training a child, the parables of seed and talents, and Mary Wollstonecraft on the education of women. Other voices raise the standing questions: whether nature is good, blank or stubborn; whether a school frees or cages; whether growth can be forced; whether effort or grace does the work.
questions: The readings put the training of character before the acquiring of knowledge. What would a school or a home look like that took that order seriously?
Confucius says people are alike by nature and differ by practice; Locke calls the mind white paper; Mencius says nature tends to good. Which picture of a child do you find truest?
One reading says that changing even one trait after maturity is nearly impossible. What has your own experience of trying to change taught you?
Mill fears a state education that moulds everyone alike, and Blake a school that cages the bird. How can education develop each child's particular aptitude?
The readings say capacity grows by effort and also that bounty is given beyond desert. Where in your own learning have you seen each?

outside.why: Plato held that the power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already, and that education turns the whole soul toward the light.
Proverbs says: train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.
A sage who grew up among the sages said that study is not the most important thing, but actions.
Paul says that knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth, and that whoever thinks he knows anything knows nothing yet as he ought.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein says: learn from me how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge. What kind of training has to come before knowledge for knowledge to be safe?
The Great Learning says that when persons are cultivated families are regulated, then states rightly governed, and the whole kingdom made tranquil.
Juvenal advised his readers to pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
The first letter to Timothy says that bodily exercise profiteth little, but godliness is profitable unto all things.
The Letter to the Ephesians speaks of teachers given for the perfecting of the saints, till we all come unto a perfect man.
Mencius said that that whereby man differs from the lower animals is but small; the mass of people cast it away, while superior men preserve it.
Jeremiah asks: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. Is there an age after which a character can no longer be changed?
Plato said that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially with a young and tender thing, for then the desired impression is more readily taken.
Proverbs says that though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar, yet will not his foolishness depart from him. Are there people whom no education can reach?
Luke says of the boy Jesus that he increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.
In the parable a man gave talents to his servants, to every man according to his several ability.
John Stuart Mill called a general State education a mere contrivance for moulding people to be exactly like one another. How can schooling serve each child's aptitude and not a single mould?
Paul says: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
Aristotle taught that we become builders by building and just by doing just acts.
Paul says: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God which worketh in you.
Confucius said: by nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.
Malachi speaks of one who is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap.
Paul says that we, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image.
Mencius taught that human nature tends to good as water tends to flow downwards. If nature is good, is education a drawing out or a making over?
Locke supposed the mind to be white paper, void of all characters, and all its furniture from experience. Is a child a blank page, a seed, or a mine of gems?
Isaiah says that the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
Nelson Mandela wrote that people must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.
The first psalm likens the blessed man to a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season.
Jesus said: I am the vine, ye are the branches; he that abideth in me bringeth forth much fruit.
Proverbs describes an untended field, all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof.
Explaining the parable of the soils, Jesus said: the seed is the word of God.
Hosea says: break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the Lord, till He come and rain righteousness upon you.
In the parable some seed fell among thorns, and the thorns sprung up and choked it.
Jesus said: seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
Jesus said: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.
The Qur’an speaks of a messenger sent to recite revelations, to purify, and to teach people that which they knew not.
Emerson's counsel was: trust thyself; every heart vibrates to that iron string. Does a person need a teacher to light the lamp, or only the courage to look within?
Paul says: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Mencius tells of a man who pulled at his growing corn to help it, and came home to find it withered. When does unceasing effort help growth and when does it harm?
The Letter to the Ephesians says: by grace are ye saved through faith; it is the gift of God, not of works.
Paul says that it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. How do a bounty earned by effort and a bounty freely given fit in one life?
Jesus said that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
The Letter to the Hebrews says that strong meat belongs to those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Jesus said that anyone who will do God's will shall know of the doctrine.
Alexander Pope placed man on an isthmus of a middle state, in doubt to deem himself a god or beast.
Aristotle said that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice he is the worst of all.
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.
Paul says that whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
The council saw that Peter and John were unlearned and ignorant men, and took knowledge of them that they had been with Jesus.
Paul heard the answer: my grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.
Milton wrote that the end of learning is to know God aright, and out of that knowledge to love Him and be like Him.
William Blake's schoolboy asks how the bird that is born for joy can sit in a cage and sing. What must a school be like to bring out a child's possibilities and not wither them?
